content.text: I found a concrete difference: the Codex handoff still asks for validation and allows development commands, while the Claude handoff leaves validation to the orchestrator. The standalone Codex run retried `verify` after sandbox failures. Those are potential sources of extra worker time, but we don’t have phase timings to quantify them.

**We haven’t reduced Codex’s workload much yet.** JEV prepares context, then launches almost the same full Codex job.

Three factors stand out:

- **Codex still handles validation.** Our [Codex prompt](/home/peterc/jev-orchestrator/src/agents/codex.ts:19) asks for changes and validation. The standalone run retried `verify` twice after sandbox failures; the JEV worker also reported sandbox trouble. JEV then runs independent checks afterward.
- **Both use Terra/high.** Prepared context doesn’t change that reasoning setting. Lower effort generally favors speed, according to [OpenAI Docs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning). Whether that explains much of these runs needs measurement.
- **This issue requires little discovery.** It already names the two files and required checks, so preparing its context offers limited work to save.

**136.0 versus 132.7 seconds shows no improvement in this pair.** We lack phase timings and repeated runs to establish the exact cause.

The next useful experiment is to give Codex an explicit implementation-only handoff, keep approved validation in JEV, and measure preparation, first edit, worker completion, and validation separately. Test lower reasoning effort as a separate variable.
